question: The Commission is proposing to extend the duty-free trade regime with Ukraine, introduced as a result of the Russian aggression, for another year until June 2025. Support for Ukraine should persist and remain a shared objective of all EU Member States. Nevertheless, duty-free imports of Ukrainian agricultural products cause a surplus of commodities in the EU, including in Czechia.

Particularly for wheat, barley and rapeseed, the cheap competition from Ukraine causes market prices to fall below production costs, i.e. farmers are forced to sell their products at a loss (even after subsidies are taken into account). This situation has been ongoing for a long time and is affecting the livelihoods of farmers, especially those focused purely on crop production.
The situation should be promptly addressed considering the new harvest contracts for 2024. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission planning to propose concrete measures to offset the negative effects of visafree trade with Ukraine for farmers in crop production?
When will the Commission propose such measures, in particular to protect European crop production farmers, and what will these measures look like?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.3.2024) Bilateral trade in goods between the EU and Ukraine is governed by the Association Agreement. However, it must be noted that imports into the EU of oilseeds are not subject to any duty, and that since 2020 the applicable import duty for maize is set at zero whatever the origin is.

Since the start of the Russian aggression against Ukraine until the end of January 2024, Czechia imported from Ukraine 111 141 tonnes of cereals and 193 549 tonnes of oilseeds1, a very small quantity compared to the total Czech production which reached 9.3 million tonnes in 2023. Prices of cereals in Czechia closely follow global prices.

They significantly dropped from their exceptional peaks of 2022 due, at that time, to the consequences of the Russian aggression against Ukraine. This surge was only temporary and prices are now back to levels observed in 2021 and similar to prices in other Member States.

As input costs also temporarily surged in 2022 and 2023, the Commission took measures to support farmers2 including partially exempting farmers from rules on land lying fallow. Since 4 June 2022, the EU has temporarily fully liberalised all imports from Ukraine under Autonomous Trade Measures3 (ATMs).

While the main objective of the ATMs is to support Ukraine, the measures are also mindful of the impact they may have on EU farmers. Therefore, the Commission proposal4 to extend the current ATMs until 5 June 2025 includes a strengthened safeguard mechanism that could be triggered in case of proven adverse effect on the market of the Union or of one or several Member States.
The Commission considers that its proposal strikes the right balance between continuing the EU’s unwavering trade support for Ukraine while safeguarding the interests of farmers in the EU.
